summary: The note warns that space weather, especially coronal mass ejections (CMEs), could threaten the undersea cables that carry about 95% of international data traffic. It uses the October 11, 2023 CME, which caused only sporadic GPS malfunctions and minor satellite disruptions, as a wake-up call. It covers expert views, expected increases in risk as the sun nears solar maximum, mitigation efforts, early warning systems, geopolitical implications, and calls for more research and collaboration.
one_line: Experts warn that CMEs and geomagnetic storms could damage undersea cables carrying most international data, urging resilience investment, early warning, and international collaboration.
key_facts: A significant coronal mass ejection (CME) event occurred on October 11, 2023, putting scientific and tech communities on alert.
A CME is a massive burst of solar wind and magnetic fields that can release billions of tons of matter at speeds exceeding one million kilometers per hour.
Undersea cables ferry as much as 95% of international data traffic.

Johnathan Graham, chief engineer at Transatlantic Comm Solutions, says the cables are built to withstand physical threats like fishing trawlers or shark bites, but their resilience against electromagnetic disturbances is limited.
The October 11 solar storm caused sporadic GPS malfunctions and minor satellite disruptions but spared most technology systems from significant harm.
Melissa Carter, Director of International Cable Operations, said "We dodged a bullet this time."
As the sun enters an active phase of its 11-year cycle, forecasters warn of a 'solar maximum' with more frequent and intense CMEs.
Companies have begun investing in technological upgrades to shield undersea cables against geomagnetically induced currents.
UNOOSA and the ITU work toward guidelines and frameworks for dealing with space weather threats.
NOAA aims to extend alert times for CMEs using more sophisticated satellites monitoring the sun's activity.
The 'Solar Shield' project is led by a consortium of cable operators and space agencies.
Dr. Haruto Takahashi says countries and companies that invest in space weather resilience will have a clear advantage in economic and security standing.
ESA and NASA continue research on space weather forecasting mechanisms.
